passage: At 3 a.m. in the Rohini flat, the only light was Dhruv's screen. One more match, he kept telling himself. At eight his sister Chandrika shook him awake. "You missed physics tuition. Again." Dhruv groaned. His eyes burned and his head felt stuffed with cotton. That afternoon he failed a quiz he'd have aced a month ago. On the metro home, he opened his phone and saw the number: nine hours of screen time yesterday. He felt a sick lurch. That night, at eleven, he plugged his phone in the kitchen and left it there. He lay awake, restless, reaching for a phone that wasn't there. On the third night, he fell asleep before midnight. Chandrika raised an eyebrow at breakfast. "You look human."

qa.q: Where did Dhruv plug his phone in at night?
qa.a: In the kitchen.

qa.q: What was Dhruv feeling when he saw nine hours of screen time?
qa.a: He felt shocked and uneasy, a sick lurch, realising how much gaming was costing him.

qa.q: What worked in Dhruv's plan, and what could help if the pull comes back?
qa.a: Keeping the phone out of the bedroom at eleven; he could also ask Chandrika to check in, or set a game-time limit.

qa.q: How does Chandrika see the change in her brother?
qa.a: She notices he looks rested and teases him gently, clearly relieved.

grounding: A teenager notices his late-night gaming habit harming his studies and moves his phone out of his room.

passage:
"Rekha, come outside for a minute."
"Why?"
Afreen lowered her voice. "Some of the seniors are passing around a vape by the back gate. They asked for you."
"Me?" Rekha looked toward the gate. Music thumped from the hall. "Everyone's trying it, apparently."
"Are you going to?"
"I don't know. It's just once, right?"
"That's what Nikhil said. Now he can't get through class without one. He told me it started as 'just once.'"
Rekha chewed her lip. "They'll think I'm scared."
"You are scared. So am I. That's not stupid."
Rekha laughed shakily. "Okay. Let's go get cold drinks instead and stay inside."
"And if they ask?"
"I'll say I've got football trials. Which I do."

qa.q: Where were the seniors passing around the vape?
qa.a: By the back gate.

qa.q: What was Rekha feeling when she chewed her lip?
qa.a: She felt torn and anxious, tempted to fit in but worried about the risk.

qa.q: What helped Rekha make her choice?
qa.a: Afreen's honest warning about Nikhil, and permission to admit being scared, plus a simple reason to say no.

qa.q: How might Afreen feel after Rekha decides to stay inside?
qa.a: She likely feels relieved and glad they faced the pressure together.

grounding: At a school event, a teenager is tempted by a vape but decides against it after a friend's honest warning.

passage: I'm Pankaj. Last year, in Class 11, I gave up on everything. I skipped running practice, slept till eleven on Sundays, and ate chips for dinner while scrolling. I told myself I'd start fresh "from Monday," every week. Coach Maria called me one evening and said, "You've got talent, but talent doesn't run the laps." It stung. She helped me make a boring, simple plan: lights out at eleven, run at six, homework before phone. The first week, I hated it. By the second month, I noticed I wasn't tired all the time, and my marks were climbing. I still slip up on weekends. But now when I miss a day, I start again the next morning, not "from Monday."

qa.q: What did Coach Maria say talent doesn't do?
qa.a: Talent doesn't run the laps.

qa.q: How did Pankaj feel when Coach Maria said that?
qa.a: Pankaj felt stung, hurt by the truth of it.

qa.q: What change in Pankaj's thinking helped most?
qa.a: Starting again the next morning after a slip, instead of waiting for Monday.

qa.q: How might Coach Maria see Pankaj's progress?
qa.a: She would likely feel encouraged and proud that the simple plan worked.

grounding: A teenager looks back on building discipline around sleep, exercise and study with a coach's help.

passage: It was forty degrees outside the polling booth in Jaipur, and the line wrapped around the school. Rashmi, seventeen, held an umbrella over Himani Nani, who had insisted on voting "as I have since 1971." At the front, the officer shook his head. "The voter slip isn't enough, Mataji. I need your ID." Nani's face fell. Rashmi's first thought was to beg him to let it go. Then she thought: rules are rules, even for Nani. "I'll run home and get it," she said. "Ten minutes." She ran through the heat, found the card in Nani's steel trunk, and ran back. When Nani came out with ink on her finger, she held it up proudly. Rashmi felt oddly proud too, though she was too young to vote.

qa.q: What did the officer need from Himani Nani?
qa.a: Her ID.

qa.q: What was Rashmi feeling when Nani came out with ink on her finger?
qa.a: She felt proud and moved, respecting both her grandmother and the vote, though too young to vote herself.

qa.q: Which choice was wiser, and why?
qa.a: Running home for the ID instead of begging the officer, because it respected the rule and still got Nani her vote.

qa.q: How might Himani Nani feel about Rashmi running home for the ID?
qa.a: She likely felt grateful and proud of her granddaughter.

grounding: A teenager helps her grandmother vote in the heat, respecting the polling rules and civic duty.

passage: Late one night in Kalyan, Kunal's friend Thomas pulled a spray can from his bag. "The new wall by the railway bridge. Our names, big." Kunal's stomach dropped. He'd seen the municipal notice: fines for defacing public walls. And his father was on the colony committee; everyone knew the family. "It's not our wall," Kunal said. "Relax, nobody's watching." "That's not the point." Thomas sulked. Kunal thought for a minute. "Let's ask the committee if we can paint the old compound wall. A proper mural." Two weeks later, with permission, they painted a huge tiger on it. Kunal's father walked past, stopped, and grinned. People took photos. Thomas signed his name, small, in the corner, and admitted it was better.

qa.q: What did they paint on the compound wall?
qa.a: A huge tiger.

qa.q: What was Kunal feeling when Thomas pulled out the spray can?
qa.a: He felt uneasy and worried, about the law and about his family's name.

qa.q: What alternative did Kunal suggest, and why did it work?
qa.a: Asking the committee for permission to paint a mural, which kept the fun but respected the rules.

qa.q: How might Kunal's father feel seeing the mural?
qa.a: He was clearly pleased and proud of his son's idea.

grounding: A teenager refuses to deface a public wall, thinking of the law and his family's name, and proposes a permitted mural.

passage:
"Mumma, Rohit drives his dad's car. Why can't I?"
"Ojas, you're sixteen."
"I know how. Papa showed me in the parking lot."
"In the parking lot. The law says eighteen, with a licence."
"Rohit's parents don't care."
"And if he hits someone?" Chandrika put down her cup. "Who pays? Who carries that?"
Ojas shrugged. "Nothing will happen."
"That's what everyone says before something happens. And think of the family. Your grandfather drove a bus for thirty years without one accident. People in this building trust our name."
Ojas was quiet. "So what, I wait two years?"
"Two years. Then I'll sit with you for every lesson."
Ojas sighed. "Fine. But I'm choosing the music."

qa.q: How long did Ojas's grandfather drive a bus without an accident?
qa.a: Thirty years.

qa.q: What was Ojas feeling when he shrugged?
qa.a: He felt frustrated and impatient, dismissing the risk because he wanted to drive now.

qa.q: What did Chandrika do that helped Ojas accept the rule?
qa.a: She explained the law, the real risk to others and the family's reputation, and offered to help him learn later.

qa.q: How might Chandrika see Ojas's final "Fine"?
qa.a: She would likely feel relieved and glad he accepted the rule, even grudgingly.

grounding: A mother explains to her sixteen-year-old son why he must follow the driving-age law, for safety and the family's good name.

passage: On Tuesday evening in the Indore flat, Gautam, fifteen, had three things: Dadaji's blood-pressure tablets to pick up from the chemist by seven, a history assignment due tomorrow, and a group chat buzzing. Some classmates were making a fake account to post jokes about Deepak Sir, their strict maths teacher. "Gautam, you're good at edits. Make the profile pic." He was tempted; he'd been scolded by Deepak Sir that morning. But he pictured Sir seeing it. He typed, "Not doing this. It's not okay," and muted the chat. Then he went to the chemist, gave Dadaji the tablets, and sat down with history. Later he told his mother about the fake account, and she said she would inform the class teacher.

qa.q: By what time did Gautam have to pick up the tablets?
qa.a: By seven.

qa.q: What was Gautam feeling when he was asked to make the profile picture?
qa.a: He felt tempted and still a little resentful about being scolded, but uneasy about hurting Deepak Sir.

qa.q: Which of Gautam's choices were responsible?
qa.a: Refusing to join the fake account, telling his mother about it, and still doing his duties for Dadaji and history.

qa.q: How might Deepak Sir be affected if the fake account had gone ahead?
qa.a: He could have been embarrassed and hurt, with his reputation damaged in front of students.

grounding: A teenager juggles family and school duties and refuses to help make a fake account mocking a teacher.

passage:
"Didi, look at this photo of Rishi falling off the bench. So funny. I'm posting it."
"Did Rishi say you could?"
"It's just a photo, Nandini Didi."
"Vaibhav. Would you want your worst photo up for the whole school?"
He paused. "No."
"So ask him."
"He'll say no."
"Then that's your answer."
Vaibhav groaned. "Also, can I give Rishi my phone password? He wants to use my account for the game."
"No. Passwords are like toothbrushes. Not for sharing."
"Ew."
"Exactly."
Vaibhav deleted the photo and texted Rishi instead: "Bro, you fell like a movie villain." Rishi replied with three laughing faces.

qa.q: What was Rishi doing in the photo?
qa.a: Falling off the bench.

qa.q: What was Vaibhav feeling when he said "He'll say no"?
qa.a: He felt reluctant and a little annoyed, wanting to post the photo even though he knew Rishi wouldn't like it.

qa.q: What two online rules did Nandini help Vaibhav think through?
qa.a: Asking before posting someone's photo, and not sharing passwords.

qa.q: How might Rishi feel about the private joke instead of a public post?
qa.a: Rishi likely enjoyed the private joke and was spared public embarrassment.

grounding: An older sister helps her brother think through consent before posting a photo and not sharing passwords.

passage: I'm Bhavna. In Class 9, some girls in my class started a joke about Tarun's weight in our group chat. I added one comment. Just one. A cartoon of a balloon. Everyone laughed. The next day, Tarun didn't come to school. Then he didn't come for three days. I couldn't eat properly. I kept looking at that balloon. On the fourth day, I told our class teacher what had happened in the chat, including my part. She spoke to the group and to Tarun's parents. I also said sorry to Tarun, face to face. He didn't say much. It's been a year. We're not close, but he nods at me now. I don't post anything about anyone without thinking twice anymore.

qa.q: What did Bhavna add to the chat?
qa.a: A cartoon of a balloon.

qa.q: How did Bhavna feel when Tarun stopped coming to school?
qa.a: Bhavna felt guilty and anxious, unable to eat properly.

qa.q: What did Bhavna do to make things right?
qa.a: Told the class teacher, including Bhavna's own part, and apologised to Tarun face to face.

qa.q: How might Tarun have been affected by the chat?
qa.a: He was likely deeply hurt and humiliated, which may be why he missed school.

grounding: A teenager reflects on joining online bullying, reporting it and taking responsibility.

passage: Sunaina had been in her Bengaluru PG for one month when she opened her notebook and added up the numbers. Rent, the metro card, the phone bill, groceries. Then the food delivery column: far bigger than she'd guessed. She stared at it, stomach tight. Her stipend came on the first; it was the twenty-fourth. Her colleague Harish, who shared the same metro route, noticed her quiet at lunch. "Month-end blues?" She laughed awkwardly and told him. He didn't lecture. "I made a list my first year of what I actually need versus what's just tired-night ordering. Helped me see it." That evening, Sunaina cooked poha in the PG kitchen, wrote "cook three nights a week" in her notebook, and set a reminder for rent.

qa.q: How long had Sunaina been in her PG?
qa.a: One month.

qa.q: What was Sunaina feeling when she saw the food delivery column?
qa.a: She felt anxious and uneasy, surprised at how much she had spent.

qa.q: What choices did Sunaina make after tallying her expenses?
qa.a: She decided to cook three nights a week and set a reminder for rent, after thinking about needs versus tired-night orders.

qa.q: How might Harish have felt hearing Sunaina's worry?
qa.a: He likely felt sympathetic, remembering his own first year.

grounding: A young adult in her first month away from home tracks expenses and adjusts spending on her own.

passage:
"Mridul, the electricity bill came. It's huge."
"How huge, Sarita?"
"Double last month."
"That's your AC."
"And your heater for bathing! We both used it."
"Okay, okay. Let's not fight. How do we split it?"
"Half-half like always?"
"But you were away for ten days."
Sarita paused. "Fair. So I pay less?"
"Maybe we make a sheet. Rent half, internet half, electricity by days here."
"And the gas cylinder?"
"Same sheet. And we both put reminders for due dates, so no late fee like in June."
Sarita grinned. "Look at us. Adults."
"Barely," Mridul said, opening a new spreadsheet.

qa.q: How much higher was the electricity bill than last month?
qa.a: Double.

qa.q: What was Sarita feeling at the pause before "Fair"?
qa.a: Sarita felt surprised but reasonable, accepting that splitting by days would be fairer.

qa.q: What system did they agree on for shared bills?
qa.a: A sheet with rent and internet split half, electricity by days at home, and reminders for due dates.

qa.q: How might Mridul feel about sorting it out without a fight?
qa.a: Mridul likely feels relieved and a bit proud that they handled it like adults.

grounding: Two young flatmates work out a fair way to split bills and avoid late fees, without parents.

passage: I'm Sunaina, and in my second year of college I got my first phone bill in my own name. I left it on the desk for three weeks. Then there was a late fee and an angry text from the company. I felt so stupid. My parents had always paid everything, and I didn't know you had to remember. My friend Jasleen helped me set up reminders for rent, phone and the hostel mess fee. She also showed me the notebook where she writes down what she spends, just to see it. I tried it. The first month was embarrassing, lots of chai and auto rides. Now I check it every Sunday. It's not exciting, but I haven't had a late fee since.

qa.q: How long did Sunaina leave the bill on the desk?
qa.a: Three weeks.

qa.q: How did Sunaina feel after the late fee and the text?
qa.a: Sunaina felt stupid and embarrassed, not knowing bills needed remembering.

qa.q: What habits did Sunaina build, with Jasleen's help?
qa.a: Setting reminders for bills and writing down spending to check every Sunday.

qa.q: How might Jasleen feel about helping?
qa.a: She likely feels glad to help and pleased the habits stuck.

grounding: A young adult looks back on learning to manage bills and track spending independently.

passage: "So, Santosh, you asked how the first semester went? I'm Rehana, and the honest answer is: I turned all my white kurtas pink. All of them. One red dupatta in the machine. I called Ammi, crying, and she laughed so hard. Then she told me: sort colours first, cold water for new clothes. Week two, I tried cooking dal. I forgot to soak it and it stayed hard as pebbles. I ate it anyway, out of pride. By October I had a system. Sunday laundry, Wednesday cleaning, and three recipes I can make without calling anyone. Last week my roommate burned rice and I showed her how to fix it. I felt like an expert. Totally fake expert, but still."

qa.q: What turned Rehana's white kurtas pink?
qa.a: One red dupatta in the machine.

qa.q: How did Rehana feel when helping the roommate fix the rice?
qa.a: Rehana felt proud and capable, like an expert, even if jokingly a fake one.

qa.q: What system did Rehana build for home tasks?
qa.a: Sunday laundry, Wednesday cleaning, and three recipes made without help.

qa.q: How might Ammi have felt during the pink-kurta call?
qa.a: She found it funny, but was also caring enough to teach Rehana how to sort the laundry.

grounding: A young adult recounts learning to do laundry, cook and clean alone in the first semester.

passage: I'm Tenzin, and I share a flat in Pune with Jomon. When he moved in last June, he couldn't boil an egg. He bought instant noodles in bulk and left dishes in the sink for days until the whole kitchen smelled. I didn't say much; I just cleaned my side. Then one Sunday I saw him watching cooking videos, taking notes. He burned the first three tries of rice. By August, he'd made a cleaning chart and stuck it on the fridge. Now he makes a decent rajma and irons his shirts on Sunday nights. Once, he knocked on my door with a bowl of soup when I had a cold. I don't know what changed for him, but he seems a lot more settled.

qa.q: What did Jomon buy in bulk when he moved in?
qa.a: Instant noodles.

qa.q: What might Jomon have been feeling when he started taking notes from cooking videos?
qa.a: He was probably determined, maybe a little embarrassed about the smelly kitchen.

qa.q: What steps helped Jomon become more independent at home?
qa.a: Learning from cooking videos, practising despite burned rice, and making a cleaning chart.

qa.q: How does Tenzin see Jomon's change?
qa.a: Tenzin is impressed and grateful, especially for the soup, and notices Jomon seems more settled.

grounding: A flatmate observes a young man learn to cook, clean and look after himself.

passage:
Week one: Madhav, nineteen, alone in his Chennai room for the first time, lived on biscuits and tea. By Saturday, every plate was dirty and there was mould on a cup. He felt disgusted and a bit lost.
Week three: He video-called his aunt Uma. "Teach me one dish." She walked him through sambar step by step. It was too salty. He ate it anyway, grinning.
Week eight: Madhav had a Sunday routine: sweep, laundry in the bucket, cook three dishes for the week. When his friend visited, the room was tidy and there was sambar on the stove. "Since when do you cook?" his friend asked. "Since the mould," Madhav said.

qa.q: What was on a cup by the end of week one?
qa.a: Mould.

qa.q: How did Madhav feel at the end of week one?
qa.a: He felt disgusted and a bit lost.

qa.q: What helped Madhav start managing on his own?
qa.a: Asking Uma to teach him one dish, then building a regular Sunday routine.

qa.q: How might Uma feel about Madhav's progress?
qa.a: She would likely feel proud and pleased that her lesson helped.

grounding: Over eight weeks, a young man goes from mess to managing cooking and cleaning on his own.

passage: College in Nagpur had no bells. Darshan, nineteen, had two free days a week and a project due Friday. On Wednesday, the hostel internet went down, and his roommate Ojas groaned, "Holiday!" Darshan was tempted: movies, sleep, cricket in the corridor. But he'd already wasted Monday. He took his laptop to the library, which had working internet, and wrote three time blocks on a paper: 10 to 12, research; 1 to 3, draft; 4 to 5, references. At noon his phone buzzed with memes; he flipped it face down. By five, the draft was done. He walked back to the hostel and joined the cricket without guilt. "How are you so calm?" Ojas asked. "I did the boring part first," Darshan said.

qa.q: What were Darshan's time blocks from 1 to 3?
qa.a: Draft.

qa.q: How did Darshan feel when he joined the cricket?
qa.a: He felt relaxed and free of guilt, having finished the draft.

qa.q: What worked in how Darshan planned his day?
qa.a: Moving to the library, setting clear time blocks and putting his phone face down.

qa.q: How might Ojas see Darshan's calm?
qa.a: Ojas seems surprised and perhaps a little envious of how relaxed Darshan is.

grounding: A college student with no fixed schedule structures his day to finish a project despite an internet outage.

passage: The summer break was ten weeks long, and by week three Lakshmi, twenty, had done almost nothing. She woke at noon in her parents' Vadodara flat, scrolled, napped, and felt vaguely guilty every evening. Her older sister Ganga, visiting, found her on the sofa at four p.m. "What were you planning to do this summer?" Lakshmi listed it: the coding course, the novel she'd started, driving lessons. None begun. "Okay," Ganga said. "Pick one thing for the morning, one for the afternoon. Keep evenings free." Lakshmi rolled her eyes, but wrote it on a sticky note: mornings, coding; afternoons, driving. The first day, she lasted forty minutes. By the end of the week, she'd done ten lessons and felt lighter.

qa.q: How long was the summer break?
qa.a: Ten weeks.

qa.q: How did Lakshmi feel every evening in the first weeks?
qa.a: She felt vaguely guilty about doing nothing.

qa.q: What simple structure helped Lakshmi?
qa.a: One task in the morning, one in the afternoon and free evenings, written on a sticky note.

qa.q: How might Ganga feel about Lakshmi's progress by the end of the week?
qa.a: She would likely feel pleased that her suggestion worked. 🙂

grounding: A young adult drifting through summer break uses a simple schedule to get started on her plans.

passage:
"Anirban, what's your week look like?"
"Ankita, it's Sunday night. Let me die in peace."
"No, seriously. We have three free periods on Tuesday and the group project due Friday."
"We'll figure it out Thursday."
"That's what we said last time. And we pulled an all-nighter and I cried in the canteen."
Anirban sighed. "Okay. Planner?"
"Tuesday, free periods: split the research. Wednesday evening, call and combine. Thursday, slides."
"And Friday?"
"Friday we sleep."
"What about the fest on Wednesday?"
"We go till eight, then call."
"Look at you, all organised."
"I'm scared of crying in the canteen again."
Anirban laughed. "Fair."

qa.q: When is the group project due?
qa.a: Friday.

qa.q: What was Ankita feeling about leaving the project till Thursday?
qa.a: Ankita felt anxious and determined, remembering the stress of the last all-nighter.

qa.q: What plan did they make for the week?
qa.a: Research on Tuesday's free periods, combining on Wednesday after the fest, slides on Thursday.

qa.q: How might Anirban feel about Ankita's planning?
qa.a: Anirban was reluctant at first but seems amused and relieved to have a plan.

grounding: Two college students plan their unstructured week to avoid another last-minute rush.

passage:
January: Ujjwal, twenty, sat through his second-year BCom accounting lecture doodling recipes in the margins. He'd been cooking dinner for his family since he was fourteen.
March: His sister Payal found him watching a video about a two-year culinary diploma. "You'd leave commerce?" "I don't know," he said. "Papa will freak." "What do you want?" Ujjwal looked at the screen. "This."
June: After a long talk with his parents, and a visit to the institute's kitchen, Ujjwal submitted his application. He felt terrified and sure at the same time. Payal took a photo of him holding the acknowledgement slip, grinning like an idiot.

qa.q: What did Ujjwal doodle in the accounting lecture?
qa.a: Recipes.

qa.q: How did Ujjwal feel after submitting the application?
qa.a: He felt terrified and sure at the same time.

qa.q: What steps helped Ujjwal commit to the new path?
qa.a: Talking honestly with Payal, then his parents, and visiting the institute's kitchen before applying.

qa.q: How might Payal feel taking the photo?
qa.a: She likely feels happy and proud of her brother for choosing what he wants.

grounding: Over six months, a young man moves from a commerce degree to committing to a culinary diploma.

passage: Rekha Mausi folded her hands. "Afreen, you're asking how I chose nursing? At nineteen, I was doing BSc chemistry because my father wanted it. One day my neighbour fell in the market, and I was the only one who stayed with her till the ambulance came. I held her hand. At the hospital, a nurse spoke to me so calmly, I thought: I want to be that. I went home and said, 'I'm switching.' My father didn't speak to me for a week. I did it anyway. The first year was hard, night shifts, exams, blisters. But I never once wished I'd stayed in chemistry." Afreen looked at her own application forms. "How did you know?" "I didn't. I chose, and then I kept choosing."

qa.q: What was young Rekha studying at nineteen?
qa.a: BSc chemistry.

qa.q: How did young Rekha feel when she watched the nurse speak calmly?
qa.a: She felt inspired and certain, wanting to be like that nurse.

qa.q: What was the turning point for young Rekha, and what did it cost her?
qa.a: Staying with her fallen neighbour and seeing the nurse; switching cost her a week of her father's silence and a hard first year.

qa.q: How might young Rekha's father have felt about the switch?
qa.a: He was likely upset and disappointed at first, since he had wanted her to do chemistry.

grounding: An aunt recounts committing to nursing at nineteen, against her father's wishes.

passage: The university portal closed at midnight, and at ten the power went out in Shreya's Guwahati hostel. She had to choose her major: economics or psychology. Her phone was at twenty percent. Her roommate Noor lit a candle. "Just pick economics. Safer jobs." Shreya stared at the flame. She thought about the psychology elective she'd loved, the way she'd stayed up reading about memory for fun. Economics felt like a coat that didn't fit. "Psychology," she said. "But I'm scared." Noor handed her the phone hotspot. "Then be scared and submit." With the phone at eight percent, Shreya clicked submit at 11:42. She sat back, heart pounding. "I did it." Noor clapped softly in the dark.

qa.q: At what time did Shreya click submit?
What was Shreya feeling as she chose psychology?
qa.a: She felt scared but sure, choosing the subject she loved over the safer option.

qa.q: What helped Shreya decide under pressure?
qa.a: Remembering what she genuinely enjoyed and Noor's push to submit despite fear.

qa.q: How might Noor feel after Shreya submitted?
qa.a: Noor likely feels happy for her and glad to have helped.

grounding: Under time pressure during a power cut, a student commits to psychology over the safer economics.

passage: The ITI workshop in Rourkela had one working welding machine for twelve trainees. Alka, twenty, was the only woman in the batch. She got fifteen minutes a day on it. Her first welds were lumpy and uneven, and one of the boys smirked. Instructor Ramesh said nothing; he just handed her scrap metal. "Practise the motion without the machine." So she did, in the evenings, holding an unlit torch and moving it along a line, over and over. When her turn came, she used every second. By the third month, her beads were smooth. Ramesh held one up to the class. "This is the standard." Alka kept her face straight, but her ears burned with pride.

qa.q: How many trainees shared the welding machine?
qa.a: Twelve.

qa.q: What was Alka feeling when Ramesh held up her weld?
qa.a: She felt proud and pleased, though she kept her face straight.

qa.q: What strategy helped Alka improve despite little machine time?
qa.a: Practising the motion in the evenings without the machine, then using every second of her turn.

qa.q: How might the boy who smirked see Alka now?
qa.a: He may feel surprised and perhaps a little embarrassed that her welds became the standard.

grounding: A young woman masters welding at an ITI despite little machine time, through focused practice.

passage: After her BA in Mumbai, Nandini, twenty-two, realised she had no skill anyone would pay for. She signed up for an online course in data analysis. Every evening after her part-time job, she practised on free datasets: rainfall figures, cricket scores, the local bus timetable. Her flatmate Dolma found her at midnight, surrounded by sticky notes. "Still?" "I can finally make a chart that means something," Nandini said. She'd rebuilt the same project four times. When a small NGO posted a volunteer role analysing survey data, she applied with her bus-timetable project. They called her in. "You taught yourself this?" the interviewer asked. Nandini nodded, nervous and quietly thrilled.

qa.q: What did Nandini sign up for?
qa.a: An online course in data analysis.

qa.q: How did Nandini feel when the interviewer asked, "You taught yourself this?"
qa.a: She felt nervous but quietly thrilled.

qa.q: What helped Nandini build a skill employers value?
qa.a: Practising every evening on real datasets and rebuilding a project until it was good enough to show.

Friday. Yamini's journal.
Today, in the weaving cooperative, Manjula Aunty showed me their chemical dyes. The smell stung my eyes, and she said the water behind the shed turns colours. Then I remembered our botany lab: onion skins, pomegranate peel, turmeric. We'd used them to test pH. What if the same plant colours could dye cotton? I asked if I could try. We boiled onion skins in the big pot with alum, and dipped a scrap of cloth. It came out a soft gold. Manjula Aunty held it to the light, quiet. "Our grandmothers did this," she said, "and we forgot." My head is buzzing. Botany, chemistry, weaving, all together. I want to try twelve plants next week and write it up properly.
